source.title: Exploring the Impact of Instruction Data Scaling on Large Language Models: An Empirical Study on Real-World Use Cases
source.authors: Yunjie Ji; Yong Deng; Yan Gong; Yi-Ping Peng; Qiang Niu; L. Zhang; Baochang Ma; Xian-Gang Li

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream task scores across instruction-tuning data sizes, a different setting and measure from pretraining-loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The study varies instruction-tuning data size for one base model and reports downstream use-case scores. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute scaling laws, extrapolation from small pretraining runs, or compute-optimal allocation. Numeric scores appear in Figure 1 but are not stated in the text; the rows record only the textual trend descriptions. References to scaling-law work are not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study varies only instruction-tuning data size (0.2M–2M examples) for one 7.1B base model. It reports ChatGPT-judged use-case scores. It measures no pretraining loss, fits no power law, and does not vary model, pretraining-data or compute scale. V6 concerns downstream gains with pretraining scale or loss, and V5 concerns the power-law form in fine-tuning; neither is tested. The authors explicitly leave model scale to future work. Scaling-law papers (Hoffmann et al.) are only cited. The fine-tuning-data trend is a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find that hundreds of thousands of examples suffice for translation, rewrite, generation and brainstorming. More data still helps extraction, classification, closed QA and summarization. Math, code and COT stay poor and stop improving. Future work: data quality and selection, base-model scale, and task-specific training.
record.recipe_differences: The study instruction-tunes Bloomz-7b1-mt on Chinese instruction datasets of four sizes and evaluates use-case scores; it does not reproduce pretraining loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary by use case: some improve continuously, some plateau or remain poor, and brainstorming is reported to perform best at 200,000 examples.

fits_no_version.finding: For a 7.1B model, ChatGPT-judged scores rise with instruction data from 0.2M to 2M overall and on extraction, classification, closed QA, summarization and open QA. Math, code and COT plateau after 1M and stay poor. Generation plateaus after 1M. Brainstorming is best at 200k.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream use-case scores improve with instruction-tuning data size, but unevenly by task: some plateau early and some do not improve.

record.problems: Only one 7.1-billion-parameter base model is tested, with four instruction-data sizes. The study reports no uncertainty estimates for scores; numeric values are plotted but not provided in the text. The authors also note possible low quality in math, code, and COT training data.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fit.
Fine-tuning data is varied, but no loss is measured and no power-law form is fitted (only four points of judge scores).
No variation of model, pretraining or compute scale, and no relation to pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Per-use-case numeric scores for the four BELLE models; plotted only, not stated in the text.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'tests' link is rejected: the scaling axis is fine-tuning data, there is a single base model, and there is no predictability fit. The ChatGPT judge is unvalidated here, and brainstorming results may reflect judge leniency. There are no uncertainty estimates and no repeated runs.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fit in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of larger pretraining runs from smaller runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token allocation analysis.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study varies instruction-tuning data size, but does not test whether a power-law form holds for held-out loss in fine-tuning or another regime.
Tests downstream scores against instruction-tuning data size for one base model and Chinese use cases; does not test model/compute scale or predictability from pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal split, comparison of fitting choices, or fit of a single power law to the reported curves.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Classification, extraction, closed QA, open QA, summarization, and overall score across the four instruction-data sizes
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that these scores improve continuously with increasing instruction data; see r4–r8 and r13.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Math, code, and COT gains become difficult to extend and remain poor; generation improves through 1 million examples and then plateaus, rather than showing continuing improvement; see r1–r3 and r9.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The authors say the 200,000-example dataset was optimal, contrary to improvement with increasing scale; see r10.
